title: Tao close
hook: eighty-one chapters, read one a day: which one will you keep?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last chapter: true words aren't pretty, and the more the sage gives, the more the sage has. Your line was the more I give. What did you hand over? Day one thousand one hundred forty-four.

Eighty-one chapters, one a day. Some of them were a single picture: a wheel, a bowl, a valley. Some were advice for kings that turned out to fit a kitchen. A few were hard, and we said so. Now the book is shut, and the honest question is the one you'd ask after any long trip: what came home with you? Not everything. A trip leaves most of itself behind. Today is for choosing the one chapter you'll keep in your pocket, and for one more look at the image the book keeps coming back to.
screen: `EIGHTY-ONE CHAPTERS.` → `THE BOOK IS SHUT.` → `WHAT CAME HOME WITH YOU?`

segments.voice: First, where it began. Tradition says an old archivist named Lao-tzu wrote it at a border gate on his way out of the country. The book itself never says who wrote it, and never stops to argue the point. It opens by saying the Tao that can be told is not the lasting Tao, and then spends eighty chapters pointing anyway. Second, the empty places. Thirty spokes around a hub, and the wheel works because of the hole in the middle. A bowl is useful for its hollow. The valley spirit never dies. Again and again, the book sends you to look at what isn't there. Third, the low places. Rivers and seas lead the valleys because they lie lower. The good warrior serves below. A foot back instead of an inch forward. Fourth, the image under all of it: water. Chapter eight says the highest good is like water. It benefits everything and doesn't contend, and it settles in the places people look down on. Near the end, chapter seventy-eight says nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, and yet nothing does better against the hard and strong. Plain silk, uncarved wood, the infant's soft bones, the small village, the last words about acting without fighting. They're all water in different clothes. In a working day, water looks like the person in the meeting who doesn't push, and still the conversation keeps finding its way back to them.
screen: `THE BOOK THAT CAN'T BE TOLD.` · `LOOK AT WHAT ISN'T THERE.` · `THE LOW PLACES LEAD.` · `WATER UNDER ALL OF IT.` · then, large: `LIKE WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick the chapter you'll keep. Sit and let the breath come and go like a tide. Then let the pictures pass, slowly, without grabbing. A wheel's empty hub. Muddy water going clear when it's left alone. A whirlwind that doesn't last all morning. A small fish cooked without poking. A thousand-mile journey starting under your feet. Coarse cloth, jade inside. One of them will catch, the way a leaf catches on a stone. Let that be yours. Hold it lightly. The bell holds the time.
Tao close. The end of eighty-one chapters, and the image that runs through them: water, soft and low, that benefits everything and doesn't fight. Today's word.

Your line: like water. Today, when something hard is in the way, try going around it, or under it, before you push. And tomorrow, a new book: a man, a tower, and a stack of attempts. Day one thousand one hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching keep one chapter close rather than the whole book; chapter eight, where the highest good is like water, gives the book one of its steadiest images.

original.note: Chinese: the highest good is like water, from chapter eight.

trapdoor: what you thought: like water means go with the flow.
what it means: be soft, low, and useful to everything, and don't fight; that's the highest good in chapter eight.
what a scholar hears: water returns across the book, from chapter eight to chapter seventy-eight, as its steadiest image of the Tao's way.
